content.title: Colman Domingo | How to be Extraordinary
content.text: Actor, playwright, director and producer Colman Domingo is an infectious artist whose works continue to influence those around him. Hailing from Philadelphia, Domingo has since launched into an exceptional resumé of works in the art world. He caught the attention of many playing the enticing role of Ali on the HBO original Euphoria. Domingo has since gone on to to win numerous awards such as the OBIE and the Lucille Lortel Award. He also delves into the world of writing, co-writing the book for the Broadway hit Summer: The Donna Summer Musical and producing, with his AMC digital series Bottomless Brunch at Colman’s currently in production on season 3. Recently, Domingo starred in Netflix’s Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom as Cutler alongside Viola Davis, the late Chadwick Boseman, and many more stars. Later this year he will be seen in Zola, Candyman, No Remorse and God Committee. Flaunt got to chat with Domingo about his latest projects and what keeps him going as a multidimensional artist. How did you break into the art world and how has being in it changed since you started?I’ve come into this industry in a unique way—I learned to act, write, direct and produce by doing it. I have no real formal training, outside a handful of classes. What I did have was a strong curiosity, a willingness to learn from everywhere and everyone, passion, heart, and faith. I learned as a craftsman in the theater in San Francisco in the early 1990’s. The Bay Area theater was my conservatory. It gave me my sole foundation for not only creating art that matters but creating a life. I was a part of a moment with the amplification of theaters on a national scale such as Berkeley Rep, The California Shakespeare Theater, and my best friend Sean San Jose’s Campo Santo. I got in where I fit in. And that was the Bay. I am part of a very proud group of colleagues that rep the Bay such as Zendaya, Daveed Diggs and Ryan Coogler. The industry, like many, have taken huge strides when it comes to representation but I am seeing much more systemic change. Change that will be lasting. The artists have realized that you can no longer have the luxury of just being and artist for arts sake. You have to be a disrupted to the system. Challenge leadership and ask for a more diverse, equitable and inclusive environment. In every department. I am very proud that I amplify my voice across boardrooms and on committee in so many facets of our industry and so many artists are ringing the bell making impactful change from top to bottom. You are an award winning actor, playwright, director and now producer. What is it like to dip into a multitude of fields and do they intersect at all?They absolutely intersect! Developing into a writer has made me a more detailed actor and being a director has made me a more patient actor. I pride myself as a director because I have such extensive skills as an actor and writer and I can look at every aspect of not only guiding a creative team towards a vision, but I have immeasurable skills as working text and action. I have been a producer since the 1990’s as well. Starting with producing some of my early work as a playwright and founding my own theater company. I have picked up the mantel on producing even more as I have my own production company, Edith Productions, where I believe that intersectionality plays to our companies strengths. I support my Creative Director and Development Executive to dip into a multitude of fields and innovate with how we tell stories. That is essentially my ethos as an artist. Always be willing to be on the cusp of cross pollinating mediums. You never know what beautiful art that we will create. Small stories with a large impact. How has the pandemic affected your headspace and the way you create art?It has slowed me down exponentially to be even more mindful on what and how I create. I started my production company in the very beginning of the pandemic. So it has propelled me to develop work I find meaningful and build bridges in our culture. I have truly cut our the noise and focused in on what matters to me and my creative team as artists. I have included everyone on my team from agents, managers, executives, and production company to have meaningful, purposeful meetings on what we are doing. So that we are truly in the center of our purpose. I am 51 years old, I truly want to make this next chapter move the dial on our culture and I am very conscious of that. So I inspire us all to create wisely. As if our lives depend on it. Because they do. What is it like to play Ali in Euphoria, and what are some things you learned playing this role?I’ve learned to have more empathy for the disease of addiction and understand relatives who have struggled with it. I’m honored to play an ordinary human who is extraordinary in his thoughts and wisdom. He is an extremely flawed character who’s only purpose is to redeem someone else in their struggle with addiction while hopefully redeeming a small part of himself at the same time. He is part my own father, my brother, and countless men that struggle with their place in the world and have fallen into addiction. He reminds me a lot of men that I know who haven’t received a mic to tell their story. I believe Sam Levinson has created a character for the ages. What is your favorite part about playing Ali? Can you relate to him at all?I love the still nature that Ali has, which is something I definitely don’t have. There has been a conscious decision to make sure Ali is extremely mindful with his words and actions. I feel like I’m learning from Ali. He is a street philosopher. He has attained all this wisdom by making many mistakes. He’s well read, he’s an observer, but his intelligence comes all from experience not formal education. It makes me think about all the brothers who end up in the prison system and discover Islam. The Islamic religion serves as a great pragmatic practice for a healthy way of living in America.You star in the Netflix original Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom which premiered December 18th. What was it like to film this movie and what was memorable about it?It truly is a highlight of my career to work with titans in the industry such as Chadwick Boseman, Viola Davis, Michael Potts, and Glynn Turman. I’m working with actors who are at the top of their game in one incredible boxing ring. Everyone knows how to spar. And the master is George C. Wolfe, one of the greatest storytellers of our time. You know you will succeed with those heavyweights in your corner. And since this is Chad’s last film, I feel extremely lucky to be part of his legacy. Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom deals with issues of race, art, and the historic exploitation of black recording artists by white producers. What can the audience learn from the themes presented in the film?Especially at the end of 2020, where there has been literal fires in the street raging against systemic racism in our country. This film provides a great meditation on the soul of America and Black people in America. It’s about the Blues, and the Blues tell the story of African Americans in America. So I think it’s a great tool for us to reexamine our history and our place in it—people of every hue, gender, background, religion. We tackle that deeper, meaningful conversation that we all need to have in these times. Did you encounter any challenges or hardships while filming Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom?It was an arduous rehearsal period that required everything from us. I had to learn to play the trombone—which I think is one of the more difficult instruments. I gained a good 10 pounds, because George said I looked too young next to Chadwick. So I stopped working out and started eating. Doing an August Wilson play will take everything you got. You will sink into depression, doubt your skills, question everything because it’s required. But when you’re in it, and the scene is working, there is no better feeling. That’s what August Wilson gives to Black artists with his work.Are there any scenes in particular that you liked filming or felt were important?I thought it was very important to show some tenderness with Viola Davis’s Ma Rainey. I love the scene where she explains how she feels in this systemic racist industry. My character Cutler holds space for her and lets her express her feelings in a beautiful moment. Viola and I wanted talked about Ma showing that tenderness by taking Cutler’s hand. I also love the scenes with the band. My character could be on both sides, there’s a very different energy when working with 3 men. That camaraderie is something I hold very dear to my heart.Tell me about Bottomless Brunch with Colman and what it is like to lead a project such as this?It was originally a sit-down cocktail culture show that I was developing with AMC Networks. When the pandemic hit, I thought we had a tremendous opportunity to pull the veil aside and venture into each other’s homes and connect the only way we could: with the power of Zoom. Everyone who knows me knows I throw a great party because I love connecting people. My job as the host was to connect and then to recede into the background and let the conversation flow. I wanted to reach into my phone book with my peers and have some fun and insight and let the conversation go wherever it needed to go and bring joy into people’s homes. I’m excited to say we’ll be starting season 3 very soon. You co-wrote the book for the Broadway hit Summer: The Donna Summer Musical which was honored with two Tony nominations, how is writing different from acting and directing and what is that process like?A lot of my writing happens when I am ready to have the space and my mind is clear. If I am home, I lock myself in my study, turn on the music and submerge myself in the process. If I am on the road, I put in my headphones and go at it. It is really about getting it that whole world onto paper. It is really beautiful when I am able to give myself that time and not leave the room until it is done. I can almost hear the characters’ voices out loud, I understand their inner worlds and make sure that the rules of the universe I am building make sense to me. I love the magical and surrealist and there is always an underpinning of truth to my work. The characters have to operate from an honest place. Once I am finished, the writing has a life of its own and it evolves even further once the director and actors get involved. In turn when I am the director, I feel in service to protect the writer, their vision and to make sure everyone involved is on board with it. A lot of it is connecting and making connections. There is a ton of technical things that go into prep, but the alignment of the logistics allows the creative to flourish. And as the actor, it is the rigorous preparation, the clarity of my intention and being in the moment that allows me to be the most honest in my performance. When do you feel the most invincible?When I have work laid out before me that I believe is impactful and incredible I feel like I can do anything. With the Euphoria special script, I felt like I could do anything. I also feel invincible when I have love, and I have a lot of love around me which I am very grateful for. Photographed by Jenna Jones
